I figured I'd start a new thread where we could discuss different strategies and techniques to develop our gardens. I'm already bugged out so I've been working on investing in long-term garden improvements. I added a few berry patches this year. I've tried to start mushrooms for a few years but I must be doing something wrong because I haven't seen any. I'm very blessed that my location has some established fruit and nut trees.

Word to the wise: if you plant asparagus be absolutely positively sure that you'll never want to use that location for anything else. We inherited a patch that's square in the middle of my garden and the stuff's like creeping charlie. Every time I visit my tomatoes I find new asparagus shoots.

This year I discovered a product called Tree I.V.s which are perforated plastic spikes that you pound into the ground at the base of a tree then you take a 5 gallon bucket with a gasketed hole at the bottom and place it on top. It delivers 5 gallons of water to the tree roots while minimizing runoff. I planted a few fruit trees this year and I've been pretty pleased with how they've worked so far. I'm hoping that they'll help the trees develop strong deep roots so that they're better able to survive cold winters and droughts.
Do you can your tomatoes? Last year we had so many go to waste I've decided this year to can mine so we can do easy spaghetti sauce (a very normal meal at my house)

Yes, we both can and dry tomatoes. I usually end up buying waaay too many tomato seeds in the spring when the pushers send their catalogues and my willpower is lowest due to cabin fever. That tends to lead to waaay too many tomato plants and a vow to be more sensible next year. (No luck so far but I have an extensive collection of heirloom tomato seeds.) I usually spend several weeks at the end of the summer processing a canner-full almost every evening and more on weekends. Air conditioning is a godsend. If the grid ever goes down long term I'll be building a summer kitchen post haste.

If you have the freezer space you can also freeze roma type tomatoes whole. Just lay them on a cookie sheet until they're frozen solid and seal them in a gallon ziplock. Then later you can just dump them out into the pot when you make chilli or anything else you might use whole canned tomatoes for. I was very grateful to discover that toward the end of canning season a few years ago.

I've been doing that with my bell peppers but had no idea I could do it with tomatoes. Thanks for the tip!

I don't know if I'll be able to start a garden this year, but I'm really interested in learning how to make the most of the land I have. To be honest, right now I feel really inspired by how Thoreau lived on Walden. Is that cliche? I really like the idea of finding a combination of crops that would let me live primarily out of my own garden, without requiring me to buy a large plot of land somewhere. Does anyone have experience with small, backyard type farms? What are some beginners mistakes I should avoid when I start buying seeds and planting?

You'll need to be very aware of the local elements: soil, water, sun, and temperature. What zone are you in? Find out from other gardeners in your area (in person or online) what the most common pests and diseases are and then shop for varieties that are resistant. Determine the length of your growing season and make sure that you select varieties that can finish if you have a late spring or an early fall. Learn how many hours of sun each section of your garden receives and during which part of the day. Have your soil tested. Talk to the people at your local extension office. Know your average rainfall patterns and plan for irrigation. (You can set up nonelectric drip irrigation with rain barrels if needed.) Potatoes provide the highest number of calories per acre.
This sounds like some excellent advice! Thank you so much. I'll probably spend this summer learning how to do it right, so I can try to start with a good season next year.

You're welcome. Thomas Jefferson had a lot of great quotes but one of my favorites is: "No occupation is so delightful to me as the culture of the earth, and no culture comparable to that of the garden...But though an old man, I am but a young gardener." We're all always learning and I've found that gardeners tend to be generous with time and knowledge.

Spending the rest of the summer learning and starting next year is an excellent plan. You can do some work yet this year if you're eager to get your hands in the dirt. Garlic should be planted in the fall (although you can plant it in the spring too.) You can build raised beds or till beds and add compost or other organic material. Definitely get your soil tested this year, it'll influence your planning. If you till in some manure now it'll have a chance to break down over the winter so that it won't be too "hot" and burn your plants. If you have trees that shed leaves in the fall go ahead and work them into your garden beds, they're free compost.

You can also spend the time building fences which you'll definitely want if you have any rabbits or deer in your area. If you have any interest in keeping chickens, even just 3 laying hens, check out the idea of a chicken moat around your garden. They're a pretty cool idea to keep bugs and slugs out of the garden, you can feed them garden scraps, plus you get eggs for protein.

I strongly suggest starting a dedicated garden journal with maps of your beds and notes on planting dates, finishing dates, varieties, weather observations etc. It doesn't have to be fancy, a spiral notebook will work. Start a wishlist of what you think you might want to grow and then keep notes as you try and learn different things. It'll help you rotate your crops to keep down on diseases. I can't tell you how many times I've neglected to write something down sure that I'd remember it and ended up duplicating something.
